title: React Native state, sorted
tagline: Local, server, global, navigation — and the tool each one asks for.
intro: Choosing a state library is the second question. The first is which of four kinds of state you are holding, because three of them have an answer that is not a store at all.

sections.title: Four kinds of state
sections.summary: Sort the value first; the library follows from the answer.

body: Most state arguments are really a sorting problem. A screen holds four different kinds of value, and putting one of them in the wrong place is what turns a small app into a synchronisation problem.

blocks.caption: One profile screen, and where each value belongs.

items.label: Ask who owns the truth
items.detail: The server, the app, the navigator, or this one component — every value has exactly one owner
explain: Owning means being allowed to change it. A copy that someone else keeps in sync by hand is not an owner, it is a bug waiting for a race.
The tools below map one-to-one onto the four answers, so the sorting is the decision and the library is a consequence.

items.label: Local UI state
items.detail: Is the sheet open, what has been typed — nobody outside the screen reads it, and it dies with the screen
explain: useState and useReducer, and nothing else. Reaching for a store here adds an import, a selector and a re-render for no gain.
The test is whether losing it on navigating away would even be noticed. If not, it belongs in the component.

items.label: Server state
items.detail: A copy of data the server owns: it goes stale, it can be refetched, and several screens read it
explain: It is the only kind with a lifetime you do not control, which is why it needs caching, invalidation and a refetch policy.
Putting it in Redux means writing those three by hand. TanStack Query or RTK Query is that code, already written and tested.

items.label: Global client state
items.detail: Session, theme, cart, feature flags — owned by the app, read across screens, never stale on its own
explain: This is what a store is genuinely for, and in most apps it is smaller than people expect: a token, a few settings, a draft or two.
It has no server to disagree with, so it needs no cache — only a single writer and, sometimes, persistence between launches.

items.label: Navigation state
items.detail: Which screen is showing and with which params — the navigator already stores this
explain: React Navigation keeps the route params, so copying the selected id into a store gives you two answers that can disagree.
Read it with useRoute or a selector on the navigation state, and let deep links keep working for free.

items.label: One owner, one copy
items.detail: The usual failure is server data copied into a global store, then kept in sync by hand
explain: The symptom is a screen showing an old value after another screen refreshed it, and a growing set of manual sync calls.
The fix is not more syncing. It is deciding which of the two is the owner, and having the other read from it.

items: Sort first, install second. Most 'which state library' questions dissolve once the four kinds are separated.
Server state is the majority of what a typical app displays, and the kind least suited to a plain store.
Global client state that is honestly global is usually a handful of values.

sections.title: Local state, and the cost of Context
sections.summary: useState, useReducer, and the trap that looks like a store.

blocks.caption: Where a value goes as more of the screen needs it.

items.label: useState
items.detail: One value and its setter, kept per component instance and gone when the component unmounts
explain: Batched since React 18: two setState calls in one handler produce one render, and reading the value right after setting it gives the old one.
Pass a function when the next value depends on the last — setCount(c => c + 1) — or two quick taps can end up counted as one.

items.label: useReducer
items.detail: One state object and a dispatch, for when the transitions matter more than the values
explain: Right when several fields change together, or when the same event means different things depending on the current state.
It also moves the logic out of the component into a pure function, which is testable without rendering anything.

items.label: Lift it to the parent
items.detail: Two siblings need the same value, so the nearest common parent owns it and passes it down
explain: This is the correct first move, and it stays correct for a level or two — beyond that, props travel through components that ignore them.
Lifting also widens the re-render: the parent renders, so both branches do. That is the cost that pushes people towards a store.

items.label: Context for ambient values
items.detail: Theme, locale, the current user — read in many places and changed almost never
explain: Context is a delivery mechanism, not a state manager: no selectors, no equality checks, no way to subscribe to part of a value.
That is fine precisely when the value rarely changes, which is what ambient means here.

items.label: Every consumer re-renders
items.detail: Any change to the context value re-renders every component reading it, with no way to narrow it
explain: Putting a text field's value, a timer or an animation in context re-renders half the app on every keystroke or every frame.
Memoise the value object too — a fresh {user, setUser} on each render is a new value, so consumers re-render even when nothing changed.

items.label: Split it, or use a store
items.detail: Two contexts — one for the value, one for the setters — or a store with real selectors
explain: Splitting works because setters are stable: components that only dispatch stop re-rendering when the value changes.
When you find yourself splitting a third context, that is the signal to reach for Zustand or Redux and get selectors properly.

body: Context is the most common accidental performance bug in React Native: it looks like global state, and it behaves like a prop handed to everyone at once.

sections.title: Server state belongs in a cache
sections.summary: Fetching is the easy half; staleness, retries and invalidation are the rest.

blocks.caption: One profile request, and everything the cache does around it.

items.label: useQuery(['profile', id])
items.detail: The key is the identity of the data: same key, same cache entry, wherever in the app it is used
explain: Two screens calling useQuery with the same key share one entry, so the second one renders instantly and no second request goes out.
Keys are arrays so they can be structured — ['profile', id] is invalidated by ['profile'] as a prefix, which is how a whole family is refreshed at once.
The key replaces the variable you would otherwise keep in a store, and the cache replaces the reducer that kept it in sync.

items.label: Cached data first, then a refetch
items.detail: The stale entry is returned immediately and the request runs in the background — stale-while-revalidate
explain: The user sees content on the first frame instead of a spinner, and the fresh copy replaces it when it lands.
isPending means there is nothing cached at all; isFetching means a request is in flight over data you already have. Using the wrong one is what causes flickering spinners.

items.label: staleTime and gcTime
items.detail: How long data counts as fresh, and how long an unused entry survives before it is dropped
explain: staleTime is the interesting one: it is zero by default, so every mount refetches. A few seconds removes most duplicate requests on a busy screen.
gcTime is about memory, not correctness — an entry nobody is subscribed to is dropped after it, and the next mount refetches from nothing.

items.label: Mutations, then invalidate
items.detail: A write goes through useMutation, and the keys it affected are marked stale rather than patched by hand
explain: invalidateQueries is the one line that keeps every screen consistent: they refetch on their own, and nothing has to know who else displayed the value.
Optimistic updates are the extra step when a change must feel instant — write the cache, keep the old value, and roll back if the request fails.

items.label: Refetch on focus and reconnect
items.detail: AppState and NetInfo tell the cache when the phone came back, so a backgrounded app is not showing yesterday
explain: In React Native this is wiring you have to do once: a focusManager hook on AppState, and an onlineManager hook on NetInfo.
Without it, the web defaults do nothing on a phone — window focus and the browser's online event do not exist here.

items.label: Persist for offline
items.detail: The cache is written to MMKV or AsyncStorage and restored at launch, so a cold start has content
explain: This is what makes an app usable on a train: the last known data is on screen before any request finishes, or without one at all.
Persist the queries you actually want offline, not the whole cache — and version the persisted shape so an app update does not restore something it can no longer read.

blocks.caption: A query keyed by user, and a mutation that invalidates it — the pattern almost every screen reduces to.

items: RTK Query is the same model inside Redux Toolkit, and is the better fit when a store is already there.
Once server state lives in a cache, what is left for the store is genuinely small.
Never mirror query data into a store 'so it is easier to read'. That is the synchronisation problem coming back.

sections.title: The store, once it is small
sections.summary: Redux Toolkit, Zustand, Jotai — the same subscription with different ergonomics.

blocks.caption: A token changes, and who hears about it.

items.label: One store, one writer
items.detail: Session, theme, cart — held outside the component tree so no screen owns it and every screen can read it
explain: Outside the tree is the point: unmounting a screen cannot lose the value, and two screens read the same object rather than two copies.
Keep it small. Once server data is in a query cache and route params are in the navigator, what is left is usually a handful of fields.

items.label: Redux Toolkit: slices
items.detail: createSlice generates the actions and the reducer, and Immer lets you write the update as a mutation
explain: state.items.push(item) inside a reducer is safe: Immer records the change and produces a new immutable state from it.
The value of the ceremony is traceability — every change is a named action, visible in the devtools timeline with the state before and after.
Worth it on a large app with several people in it, and heavy for a screen with a toggle.

items.label: Selectors keep renders narrow
items.detail: useSelector(s => s.cart.count) re-renders only when that value changes, not on every dispatch
explain: Selecting an object or a mapped array returns a new reference every time, so the component re-renders on every action — the classic Redux performance bug.
createSelector memoises the derived value, and useShallowEqualSelector compares field by field when you genuinely need several at once.

items.label: Zustand: the store is a hook
items.detail: create() returns a hook you call with a selector — no provider, no actions, no boilerplate
explain: useStore(s => s.token) subscribes to that slice of state alone, so the selector story is the same as Redux with a tenth of the setup.
State and the functions that change it live in the same object, which reads closer to a small class than to a reducer.

items.label: Jotai: atoms, bottom-up
items.detail: Many small pieces of state that compose, rather than one tree that everything reads from
explain: An atom is a unit of state; a derived atom is computed from others and re-renders only its own subscribers.
It suits a screen made of many independent values better than one object, and it needs no selector because the atom is the selector.

items.label: Persistence, deliberately
items.detail: MMKV or AsyncStorage keeps chosen slices across launches — and hydration is a state of its own
explain: MMKV is synchronous and much faster, which matters at startup: an async read means the first frame renders before the stored value arrives.
Persist a whitelist, never everything, and give the stored shape a version with a migration — an old payload restored into new code is a crash on launch.

rows: Big app, many people, audit trail
A few global values, little ceremony

sections.title: Where it goes wrong
sections.summary: Five habits that cost frames, and what to do instead.

blocks.caption: Why a list stutters when one row changes.

items.label: A new object every render
items.detail: style={{flex: 1}} or data={items.map(...)} builds a fresh reference each time, so memo never helps
explain: React.memo compares props by reference. An inline object or array is a new reference on every render, so the comparison always fails.
Hoist static styles with StyleSheet.create, and wrap derived arrays in useMemo with the inputs they depend on.

items.label: An inline callback per row
items.detail: onPress={() => select(item.id)} is a new function for every row, on every render of the list
explain: It defeats memo on the row component, so a thousand rows re-render because one of them changed.
useCallback on a renderItem that reads the id from its argument fixes it, and keeps one function for the whole list.

items.label: Context in the render path
items.detail: A value that changes per frame or per keystroke, read by components all over the screen
explain: Animated values belong in Reanimated's shared values, which update on the UI thread without a React render at all.
For anything else, move the fast-changing value into a store with selectors, so only the components that display it re-render.

items.label: Server data mirrored into a store
items.detail: The query cache has it, and a slice keeps a copy that some screens read and others do not
explain: Two owners means one of them is eventually wrong, usually the one a colleague forgot to update after a mutation.
Delete the copy and read from the cache. If a screen needs a transformed shape, derive it in a selector rather than storing it.

items.label: Persisted state that outlives its shape
items.detail: An old payload restored into new code, with a field that changed type or vanished
explain: The crash lands on launch, before any screen renders, and it is invisible in development because your device has the new shape already.
Version the persisted state and write a migration, or at minimum wrap the restore in a try and fall back to defaults.
